title: Refuge, again
hookLine: taking refuge once more, knowing what it means now
tomorrow: he walked away from two teachers who wanted him. what wasn't enough?

cards: Some lines get said so often they wear smooth: a pledge at school, a team chant before a game. Buddhists have one like that, in Pali, three lines, and each line is said three times.
Buddham saranam gacchami: I go to the Buddha for refuge. Then the Dhamma, the teaching. Then the Sangha, the community.
The three jewels. After years on this path, the old words come back with a sharper question inside them. When you go for refuge, where exactly are you going?

teach.b: The oldest story starts small. Soon after the awakening, two merchants on the road, Tapussa and Bhallika, offer the Buddha rice cakes and honey and ask to be his followers.
The Vinaya says they went for refuge to two: the Buddha and the Dhamma. There was no Sangha yet. The third jewel came later, when there were monks to hold it.
Now two views, both inside Buddhism.
The first says refuge points outward. You lean on a teacher who walked the whole path, a teaching you didn't make up, and friends who catch you when you wobble.
A shelter you build alone can't hold you on the day you fall apart. The second view goes to the Buddha's last journey.

To grieving Ananda he says: be an island to yourselves, a refuge to yourselves, with the Dhamma as your island. In Chan, the Platform Sutra has Huineng teaching refuge in the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha of your own nature.
On this view, a jewel outside you that never wakes anything inside you is only a nice word. Neither view throws the other out.
People chant the refuges together in one room, and then each one sits alone on a cushion.
Three jewels outside, one island inside, and the going is the practice.

how: Buddhists go for refuge by reciting the three refuges, usually in Pali and three times over, at the start of temple services, before taking precepts, and in daily chanting at home.

o: the Buddha, the teaching and the community
three vows a monk takes at ordination
three holy objects on a Buddhist shrine

games.q: the refuge, then and now — tap the pairs.
p: went for refuge to two jewels
came once there was a Sangha

s: the first lay followers took refuge in all three jewels
Tapussa and Bhallika went for refuge to two; there was no Sangha yet.
taking refuge means asking the Buddha to rescue you
refuge is turning to a teacher, a teaching and a community, and being an island to yourself.
each line of the refuge formula is said three times
the three lines are said once, then a second time, then a third.

games.q: your cousin says taking refuge is outsourcing: 'just trust yourself.' you agree with part of that. what's the best case for the other side?
o: a shelter you build alone can't catch you when you fall; a teacher, teaching and friends can.
there isn't one; the Buddha said trust yourself alone, so your cousin is right.
refuge is only a ceremony, so what it means doesn't really matter.
games.why: both views are Buddhist: be an island to yourselves, and go for refuge to the teacher, the teaching and the community. the best case for refuge outward is that nobody catches themselves alone.

practice: If you take refuge, say the three lines out loud, in Pali or English, slowly, once each, and let the sit hold the quiet after.
If you don't, say three words softly, Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha, as the names of what Buddhists lean on, and notice which one you'd reach for first.

wordCard.voice: Refuge: sarana in Pali, a shelter you go to. Three jewels to go to: the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha.

orig.note: Pali: refuge, shelter; as in Buddham saranam gacchami, I go to the Buddha for refuge.

carryVoice: The line to take with you: three jewels, a teacher, a teaching and friends on the road. That's forty-two in this block.

sources.ref: Khuddakapatha 1 (Saranattaya: the three refuges, each said three times)
